title: The Trouble With Tech Abstinence
author: The Next 30 Years
summary: This article subjects the growing school phone ban movement to careful scrutiny, drawing on a major NBER study finding that while phone bans reduce in-school device use, their effects on test scores are modest to negligible. The author argues that this research does not invalidate phone bans — phones are genuinely attention-disrupting in ways that harm classroom conditions — but it does expose an over-reliance on restriction as the primary policy lever. The central thesis is 'tech abstinence' — treating device restriction as sufficient preparation for a technology-saturated adult life — is a pedagogical dead end; students need not only to be protected from harmful scrolling but to develop the skills to use technology with purpose, agency, and critical awareness. The author distinguishes between the short-term value of bans (restoring classroom conditions for learning) and the longer-term educational need (building digital literacy and intentional technology use). The article is particularly useful for school leaders developing coherent technology policies that go beyond binary allow/ban decisions to address the deeper question of what students should know and be able to do with technology.
points: The NBER finding — phone bans reduce device use but don't significantly move test scores — suggests that the mechanism by which bans were supposed to work (improved attention → better learning) is more complicated than reformers assumed.

Phone bans are most defensible as classroom culture interventions, not learning outcome interventions: they protect the conditions in which teaching can happen, but don't directly develop the cognitive or academic skills students need.

The article's most challenging claim is that restriction-only approaches to technology leave students unprepared for adult digital life, because they never develop the competencies needed to use technology with intention and agency.

The 'tech abstinence' framing deliberately parallels abstinence-only sex education — a comparison that implies both share the flaw of expecting that restricting exposure will produce capacities that only come from guided engagement.

The implication for school policy is a both/and framework: restrict harmful passive consumption (scrolling, social media, gaming during school) while actively teaching students to use digital tools purposefully — bans without the second half are incomplete.
quotes: A major recent study [ ] from the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) examined one of the most popular [ ] school reforms of the moment: banning student cell phones. Using nationwide data from thousands of schools, researchers found that strict bans sharply reduced in-school phone use.
Student-reported feelings of well-being dipped, then improved. That pattern suggests something deeper than a simple gain or loss.

But it risks treating all screens as if they pose the same problems and offer the same educational value, or lack thereof. Schools were right to rediscover that attention matters and that not every instructional problem calls for a screen-based solution.

As instructional coach Zach Groshell recently argued [ ], the Chromebook often became less a learning tool than a classroom babysitter—a way to occupy students rather than teach them. That said, substituting activity for learning didn’t start with computers.

Schools have spent decades pretending this can be done effectively; AI does it effortlessly. I have seen AI systems give students detailed, actionable feedback on their writing—sometimes identifying weaknesses and patterns that I missed, even as a former teacher and professional writer.
It is nearly effortless on the student’s part and nearly impossible for educators to catch. AI creates a temptation for not only students but also schools.

Less prepared or motivated students may use it as a substitute for thinking, outsourcing judgment to systems they lack the knowledge to evaluate critically. In this way, AI may amplify the very inequalities it is uniquely well suited to solve.
